questions.q: A police officer parked on the roadside measures an approaching sports car at 90 km/h, while a second police car driving toward it at 60 km/h measures the same sports car at 150 km/h. Which measurement of the sports car's speed is correct?
options: Only the 90 km/h reading from the parked officer is correct
Only the 150 km/h reading from the moving police car is correct
Both are correct, because the speed of the car is relative to the velocity of the observer rather than an invariant quantity
Neither is correct, because the car has a single true speed that neither officer measured
questions.explanation: Both readings are correct: the speed of the sports car is relative to the observer doing the measuring, not an invariant quantity agreed on by all observers. The parked officer's 90 km/h is the speed relevant to a speeding ticket, but the oncoming police car genuinely measures 150 km/h.

questions.q: In special relativity, what defines an inertial reference frame?
options: A frame of reference that is accelerating relative to the Earth
A frame of reference that is not accelerating, moving in a straight line at a constant speed relative to other inertial reference frames
A frame of reference in which the speed of light is zero
Any frame of reference attached to the surface of the Earth
questions.explanation: Frames of reference that are not accelerating are called inertial reference frames. An inertial reference frame moves in a straight line at a constant speed relative to other inertial reference frames, and within it Newton's first law holds.

questions.q: What does the principle of relativity state about the laws of physics and the velocity of the observer?
options: The laws of physics change with the velocity of the observer
The laws of physics do not depend on the velocity of the observer, and there is no way to measure a vehicle's velocity without reference to something external to it
The laws of physics only hold for an observer at absolute rest
The laws of physics depend on the acceleration but not the velocity of the observer
questions.explanation: The principle of relativity states that the laws of physics do not depend on the velocity of the observer. Another way to describe it is that there is no way anyone in a smoothly moving car can measure its velocity without making reference to something external to the car.

questions.q: In classical physics established by Galileo and Newton, position and speed are relative between frames of reference. From memory, what did classical physics treat as absolute, and what does this say about rulers and clocks in different reference frames?
keyPoints: In classical physics position and speed are relative, dependent on the observer's frame of reference.
Time and space are seen as absolute: all observers agree on what a metre and a given speed are.
The rulers in one frame of reference are the same as those in another, and clocks in one frame tick at the same rate as clocks measured in another.
questions.explanation: Classical physics treats time and space as absolute even though position and speed are relative: rulers measure the same metre and clocks tick at the same rate in every frame. Special relativity is exactly the overturning of this absoluteness of time and space.

questions.q: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley used interference effects to detect changes in the time taken for light to travel through different paths in their apparatus as the Earth moved through the luminiferous aether. What did the experiment find?
options: Light travelled faster in the direction of the aether wind, confirming the aether
The predicted change in the interference pattern was not observed, as though the speed of light was unaffected by the motion of the observer or the source
The interference pattern disappeared entirely when the apparatus was rotated
Light travelled at different speeds depending on the time of year
questions.explanation: Much to their astonishment, the predicted change in the interference pattern was not observed. It was as though the speed of light was unaffected by the motion of the reference frame of its observer or its source, the famous null result.

questions.q: Axel's spacecraft fires its rockets and its velocity is measured by Effie in reference frame B to change from 50 m/s to 150 m/s over 10 s. Show that the acceleration measured in reference frame B is the same invariant value found in frame A.
questions.given: Effie (frame B) measures Axel's spacecraft velocity change from \(50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(150\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) over \(t = 10\,\mathrm{s}\)
working: This equals the \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) measured in frame A, so acceleration is invariant.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is an invariant quantity: it has the same value in all inertial reference frames. Unlike velocity, acceleration in Galilean relativity does not depend on the motion of the frame of reference.

questions.q: A plane flies at a constant speed of 200 m/s through air in which the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Find the speed of the sound relative to the reference frame of the plane in the forward direction.
questions.given: Speed of plane \(= 200\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), speed of sound in air \(= 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
working: Speed of sound relative to the plane = speed of sound in air \(-\) speed of plane
\(= 140\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in the forward direction relative to the plane
questions.explanation: Sound has a speed relative to its medium (the air). To find its speed in the plane's frame we subtract the plane's speed from the speed of sound, giving 140 m/s forward (and 540 m/s backward). This is exactly the medium-relative behaviour light does NOT show.

questions.q: A spacecraft hurtling toward Earth at 0.5c sends out a radio signal ahead of it. According to Einstein's first postulate, with what speed does the radio signal hit the Earth?
options: 1.5c, because the spacecraft's speed adds to the speed of the radio waves
c, because the radio waves travel at c regardless of the motion of the source and the receiver
0.5c, the speed of the spacecraft
It depends on whether the Earth is moving toward or away from the spacecraft
questions.explanation: Relative velocity as treated by Galileo insists the radio waves should strike Earth at 1.5c, but this does not happen. The radio waves travel at c regardless of the motion of the source and the receiver, the heart of the first postulate.

questions.q: From memory, state Einstein's two postulates of special relativity precisely, including the crucial qualifier on the light postulate. (Hint from the episode: 'Locked and Level'.)
keyPoints: Postulate 1 (Locked): the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer.
Postulate 2 (Level): all inertial frames of reference are equivalent, i.e. the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame.
The single biggest mark-loser is dropping 'the same for all observers regardless of the motion of source or observer' from postulate 1, that qualifier is the whole revolutionary content.
questions.explanation: If you stated both postulates AND kept the 'regardless of the motion of source or observer' qualifier on the light one, grade yourself Good or Easy. If you wrote only 'the speed of light is constant', grade it Again, because that omits the part that actually breaks classical physics.

questions.q: Using a thought experiment with a lamp at the centre of a moving train carriage, explain how Einstein's postulates lead to the conclusion that simultaneity is relative. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A lamp at the exact centre of a moving train carriage emits a single flash. For a passenger on the train, the light travels at c equal distances to the front and back walls, reaching both at the same instant, so the two events are simultaneous in the train's frame. For an observer on the platform the light also travels at c in both directions (first postulate), but during the time the light is travelling the train moves forward, so the back wall moves toward the flash point while the front wall moves away. The light therefore reaches the back wall before the front wall, so for the platform observer the two events are not simultaneous. Because two observers in relative motion disagree about whether the events occurred at the same time, simultaneity is relative, not absolute, and this follows directly from the constancy of the speed of light.

criteria.descriptor: Sets up the central lamp and identifies the two events as simultaneous in the train frame (equal distances at c).
States the platform observer also measures the light at c in both directions, by the first postulate.
Explains the train's forward motion makes the light reach the back wall before the front wall.
Concludes simultaneity is relative and links it to the constancy of the speed of light.

questions.explanation: The argument needs no equations, only the postulates applied carefully: the two observers disagree about timing precisely because both measure the same c.
